title: Catalog shortlist strategy & bench interpretation demo — Sapphire Systems
topics: Model catalog shortlist strategy, interpreting benchmark signals, compatibility matrix (kernels/hardware), API vs Dedicated tradeoffs, Optimize suggestions (batching/quantization)
summary: Redwood team walked Sapphire Systems through a catalog-driven shortlisting workflow. Focused on how benchmark signals map to production metrics, reading the compatibility matrix for kernels and hardware, and recommended runtime/Optimize settings for latency-sensitive endpoint. Customer raised questions about VPC/private deployment, SOC2 logs, and how to run a comparative bench on their LLM prompts. Agreed next steps: share bench spreadsheet, schedule a 2-hour follow-up to scope a short pilot, and provide security documentation.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're on for 50 minutes, we tried to keep it tight. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Ethan our solutions engineer. quick intro from your side?
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: Hi, Lena here, head of ML at Sapphire Systems — we own the model selection work.
[00:18] Marcus Nguyen: Marcus infra, I'll own any VPC or deployment questions.
[00:22] Priya Sharma: Priya, product manager, mostly around latency targets and cost impact.
[00:28] Ethan Reynolds: Great, Ethan SE. we'll demo the catalog shortlist flow, how benches are interpreted and how the compat matrix helps pick runtime variants.
[00:36] Maya Patel: Quick agenda: 1) catalog shortlisting—filters and heuristics, 2) reading bench signals and caveats, 3) compatibility matrix mapping kernels/hardware, 4) Optimize recommendations and final Q&A.
[00:48] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. our key success criteria: sub-200ms P95 for chat on 2k context, cost under our current budget, and no sensitive data leaving our VPC if possible.
[00:59] Maya Patel: Perfect, we'll keep that front of mind.
[01:06] Ethan Reynolds: Jumping in — here's the catalog page, filters on model family, tokenization type, memory footprint. note that open models are tagged with verified bench profiles and a confidence score — that's based on our internal benchset and kernel mapping.
[01:26] [screen share noise, audio glitch]
[01:34] Ethan Reynolds: You can see we surface sequence-length-specific throughput and latency ranges — so for your 2k context we recommend looking at the 2k column rather than the default 512.
[01:50] Priya Sharma: Quick question — how often are these bench numbers refreshed? last year we'd seen stalls as model patches changed.
[01:57] Ethan Reynolds: Good question. we run nightly micro-benchmarks for kernel mismatches, and full bench sweeps weekly for major model updates. but if you care about a pinned commit we recommend running a short on-prem bench with your prompt set.
[02:12] Lena Ortiz: That's what we want — run with our prompts. how painful is that?
[02:17] Maya Patel: We usually provide a bench spreadsheet and a small runner. it can be done in a few hours for a shortlist of 3-5 models. we'll share the runner config.
[02:28] Marcus Nguyen: For private deployment, we need to confirm HSM/KMS integration and audit logs — what's the flow?
[02:36] Ethan Reynolds: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and can stream audit logs to your SIEM. There was a note that in some transcripts the logs are called 'audit trail' or 'event feed' depending on infra — apologies for any naming mismatch.
[02:56] [laughter]
[03:02] Maya Patel: Now the compatibility matrix — we map model ops to kernel families (fast attention, flash-attn variant, quantized kernels). on the matrix you can filter by hardware type (A100, H100, L4) and by quantization path (fp16, 4-bit).
[03:23] Ethan Reynolds: Important nuance: a model might run on H100 with fp16 quickly, but the same model's 4-bit quantization path might only be safe for math-heavy tasks, not instruction-following with long context. bench signals include an accuracy delta column we call "regression risk".
[03:45] Priya Sharma: How do you measure regression risk?
[03:49] Ethan Reynolds: It's a prompt-set-based delta on our eval suite; think of it as a red flag metric — if it's > 5% for your LLM tasks we recommend keeping a higher precision path.
[03:58] [00:04:00] Maya Patel: Let's walk a live shortlist — we applied your filters earlier (open-license, <=16GB mem footprint, good chat coherence). here's three candidates: OpenVista-7B, Meridian-1.5B, and Harbor-13B-quant.
[04:17] Lena Ortiz: That Harbor-13B-quant jumped out; how does the latency look at 2k?
[04:23] Ethan Reynolds: On our benchmarks Harbor-13B-quant hits ~160ms median on L4 with 4-bit path and continuous batching size 4, but P95 climbs to about 300ms depending on request burstiness. That's where Optimize suggestions help.
[04:40] Marcus Nguyen: What is continuous batching?
[04:43] Ethan Reynolds: It's our runtime feature that holds short windows of requests to form optimal micro-batches without impacting median latency drastically. You can tune window size and max batch.
[04:53] Priya Sharma: If we tune for P95 under 200ms would that blow up cost?
[04:58] Ethan Reynolds: There's a tradeoff — smaller batching and higher fp precision increase unit cost. Our Optimize module provides simulations: it will show token cost vs latency for a given traffic pattern.
[05:10] [05:10] Maya Patel: Quick aside — we've seen customers try a model that looked great on bench but regressed when prompts included table parsing; that's often tokenization differences or missing post-training alignment. so hands-on benching with your prompts is high value.
[05:26] Lena Ortiz: Understood. can Redwood's bench runner preserve prompt order and replicate multi-turn history?
[05:32] Ethan Reynolds: Yes, runner supports multi-turn sequences and will push state through KV cache paths to reflect production behavior. small caveat: some bench runners approximate the KV cache; we'll note that in the spreadsheet.
[05:47] [screen flicker]
[05:55] Maya Patel: Now the compatibility matrix shows kernel health. see Harbor-13B-quant marked as 'beta' on A100-4bit kernel. that means we have optimized kernels but haven't yet rolled full regression tests for instruction tasks.
[06:12] Marcus Nguyen: So we probably shouldn't pick it for customer-facing latency-critical flows until it's GA?
[06:16] Ethan Reynolds: Correct — an option is to route production traffic to an fp16 variant on A100, with Canary fallback to the 4-bit variant during off-peak — Redwood's routing policies can do that automatically.
[06:29] Priya Sharma: How do we set up routing rules in the Console?
[06:33] Ethan Reynolds: In Console you create a route, set SLO targets, and add fallbacks by cost/latency tiers. We'll demo that quickly.
[06:41] [screen share shows Console, clicking flows]
[06:47] Ethan Reynolds: Here's a route: primary Harbor-13B-fp16 on A100, secondary Harbor-13B-4bit on L4 when latency SLA allows. You can define percent-based canaries and automatic fallback on P95 breaches.
[06:59] Lena Ortiz: Does the fallback preserve session KV cache?
[07:03] Ethan Reynolds: The runtime manages KV cache compatibility for model variants when they share tokenizer and architecture; otherwise you get a cache miss and a cold start — we flag those transitions.
[07:14] [07:14] Maya Patel: Security question?
[07:16] Jules Carter: Jules, security. What about data residency and 'no data leaves VPC' requirement — is there an on-prem package?
[07:23] Ethan Reynolds: Yes, Private deployment supports an air-gapped package with local inference nodes and a control plane that can be collocated or hosted with strict routing. We support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs to your SIEM. For KMS we integrate with AWS KMS and external HSMs.
[07:41] Jules Carter: Are SOC2 artifacts available?
[07:44] Maya Patel: We'll share SOC2 and ISO27001 docs in the follow-up.
[07:48] Lena Ortiz: Great.
[07:53] Ethan Reynolds: Back to Optimize — we have recommendations like increasing prefix cache retention, enabling KV caching for repeated multi-turn, and suggested batch windows. here's an Optimize simulation: with your traffic profile (you provided a 30req/s baseline) the tool projects a 22% token cost reduction when enabling prefix caching and 4-bit fallback for non-sensitive routes.
[08:19] Priya Sharma: How reliable is the 22%? are there caveats?
[08:22] Ethan Reynolds: It's a projection using our cost model; caveats include your actual token distribution and how often cache hits occur. If your prompts are highly unique, benefits drop.
[08:34] Marcus Nguyen: Any network implications for prefix caching in a VPC setup?
[08:38] Ethan Reynolds: Network overhead is minimal; cache lives in the runtime nodes. For Private, ensure low latency links between control plane and compute if you use a split control plane.
[08:52] [08:52] Maya Patel: Let's role-play a bench interpretation — open the bench sheet I shared earlier.
[08:58] [screen share shows spreadsheet; numbers read aloud]
[09:04] Ethan Reynolds: Row for OpenVista-7B: coherence score 0.82, latency median 85ms at 512, 210ms at 2048, regression risk 1.5%. Meridian-1.5B: cheap but lower coherence on dialog. Harbor-13B-quant: best coherence but riskier on long-context instruction delta.
[09:28] Lena Ortiz: Coherence score — is that human-rated?
[09:31] Ethan Reynolds: It's a mixed metric: automated evals plus a small human spot-check sample; it's meant to be directional.
[09:39] Priya Sharma: Which of these would you recommend for a customer support chat with lots of tabular outputs?
[09:45] Ethan Reynolds: For tabular outputs I'd avoid 4-bit variants unless you can validate on your prompt set — 13B fp16 or a mid-sized 7B with good tokenizer alignment often work better. We'll help you run a targeted bench for table parsing tasks.
[10:00] Marcus Nguyen: Operationally, if we start on Hosted API for quick test and later migrate to Dedicated or Private, how disruptive is the switch?
[10:08] Maya Patel: We design the API and routing to be consistent across Hosted, Dedicated, Private. Customers usually run a Pilot on Hosted with pinned model versions, then move to Dedicated with minimal code changes — mostly config and credential swaps.
[10:23] Lena Ortiz: Timeline-wise we want to pick shortlist this quarter and pilot next quarter.
[10:29] Maya Patel: Good cadence.
[10:32] [silence, typing]
[10:40] Ethan Reynolds: Quick demo of the model page payoff — you can click a model and see 'bench artifact' links: raw logs, kernel mapping, and a small 'what changed' changelog. That helps with the patch/regression problem.
[10:55] Lena Ortiz: Are changelogs automatic or curated?
[10:58] Ethan Reynolds: Automatically generated from bench runs but we add curated notes for significant model updates.
[11:05] Priya Sharma: On routing again — can we route by user segment? for example higher fidelity for premium users?
[11:12] Ethan Reynolds: Yes, routing rules can be parameterized by token, header, or customer attribute. You can do percent-splits or sticky sessions.
[11:21] Marcus Nguyen: Any caution about KV cache and sticky sessions at large scale?
[11:25] Ethan Reynolds: Sticky sessions increase warm-cache affinity but can be less efficient for batching; Optimize can simulate that tradeoff.
[11:36] [11:36] Maya Patel: Call is already over 40 minutes, want to hit remaining Q&A and next steps.
[11:42] Priya Sharma: One more — what's the recommended bench sample size for reliable regression detection?
[11:48] Ethan Reynolds: For instruction-following with multi-turn, we recommend 500-1,000 prompt instances; you can start smaller for a quick signal but larger gives statistical confidence.
[11:58] Lena Ortiz: Ok, makes sense.
[12:03] Maya Patel: Recap and next steps — we'll: 1) send bench runner and spreadsheet, 2) share SOC2/ISO docs and Private deployment checklist, 3) schedule a 2-hour pilot scoping session next week, 4) propose a shortlist of config presets for your latency target.
[12:20] Priya Sharma: Good. can you also include an example routing policy for canary to fallback paths?
[12:25] Ethan Reynolds: Yes we'll include a JSON snippet and Console link.
[12:29] Marcus Nguyen: Also need estimated cost delta between fp16 and 4-bit across the pilot.
[12:33] Maya Patel: We'll add that to the bench sheet.
[12:37] [12:37] Maya Patel: Any final blockers?
[12:40] Jules Carter: Need to review encryption and retention terms but no blocker for pilot.
[12:45] Lena Ortiz: We're good.
[12:47] Maya Patel: Great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with notes and artifacts.
[12:53] [meeting ends]

Add estimated cost delta fp16 vs 4-bit to bench sheet
